title: Microfluidics in Biomedical Applications: Fundamental Principles, Fabrication Technologies, Emerging Diagnostic Platforms, Organ-on-Chip Systems, Drug Development and Future Perspectives
content: Microfluidics has emerged as an important platform for manipulating and analyzing small volumes of fluids, cells, biomolecules, and particles with high precision. Its ability to control microscale flows and integrate multiple analytical steps has enabled diverse biomedical technologies, including lab-on-a-chip, point-of-care diagnostics, organ-on-chip, and microphysiological systems. This review summarizes the fundamental principles of biomedical microfluidics, including microscale fluid dynamics, laminar flow, diffusion, and key dimensionless parameters, together with major platform formats such as continuous-flow, droplet-based, and digital microfluidics. Recent fabrication approaches, including photolithography, soft lithography, molding, laser-based methods, 3D printing, micromilling, and paper- and lamination-based techniques, are also discussed. The review highlights applications in cancer and liquid biopsy, infectious disease diagnostics, cardiovascular and neurological disorders, organ-on-chip models, drug screening and toxicity testing, pharmaceutical synthesis, drug delivery, single-cell analysis, and regenerative and reproductive medicine. Particular attention is given to the growing use of microfluidics for personalized and human-relevant biomedical research. The review further examines the major challenges associated with microfluidic biomedical systems, including fabrication reproducibility, material compatibility, biological complexity, standardization, scalability and manufacturing, clinical validation, regulatory requirements, and integration with advanced computational approaches such as artificial intelligence and machine learning. Finally, future perspectives are discussed, with particular emphasis on personalized medicine, decentralized diagnostics, human-relevant drug development, multi-organ microphysiological systems, wearable and implantable microfluidics, and automated biomedical platforms.
